slides.say: k is a positive integer with exactly three different divisors, including one and k. Given: C is equal to the square root of k. How many divisors does C have, including one and C?

So k has exactly three divisors, and C is its square root. That sounds very abstract, so first let's understand which numbers have exactly three divisors. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, with divisor pairs, and then plugging in a number.
[short pause] Divisors come in pairs that multiply to the number. Take eighteen. One times eighteen, two times nine, three times six. Six divisors, in three pairs.

A factor pair normally contributes two different divisors. If both factors are the same number, that divisor is counted only once. So most numbers have an even number of divisors. When can the count be odd? Only when one divisor has no partner, because it pairs with itself. Sixteen. One times sixteen, two times eight, and four times four. Four is counted once, so sixteen has five divisors, one, two, four, eight and sixteen.
And a divisor that pairs with itself, times itself, gives the number. So an odd number of divisors means a perfect square.

slides.say: Now exactly three divisors. That's one pair, one times k, plus one middle divisor that pairs with itself. Call the middle divisor d, so d times d is k.

And what are d's own divisors? Anything that divides d also divides k. k has only three divisors, one, d and k, and k is too big to divide d. So d has only one and itself. So d is a prime, and k is a prime squared.
For example, forty-nine. One, seven and forty-nine, three divisors, and seven is a prime.

We now know the type of number C is. The question asks how many divisors C has, rather than how many divisors k has. So C, the square root of k, is that middle prime. And a prime has exactly two divisors, one and itself. So two, choice number two is our answer.
